fuller.text: This is a long essay by Gwern about GPT-3, a text-predicting AI that OpenAI announced in May 2020. It uses GPT-3 to argue for the scaling hypothesis. That is the idea that simple neural networks, just made much bigger and fed more data and computing power, keep gaining new abilities. Taken to its end, the hypothesis says this route could lead to human-level general AI.

fuller.text: GPT-3 has 175 billion parameters, the adjustable numbers a network tunes as it learns, making it 117 times larger than GPT-2. It was trained only to guess the next word in Internet text. Yet it can do arithmetic, translate, unscramble anagrams and solve analogies after seeing just a few examples in its prompt. The author calls this meta-learning: learning how to learn a new task on the spot, which nobody built in.

fuller.text: The piece says this matters because the gains from size have not slowed down. GPT-3's improvement still follows the same smooth curve seen in much smaller models. Training reportedly cost around $5 million, cheap by government or business standards. So the author expects models with trillions of parameters to be affordable, with many benchmarks perhaps falling by 10 trillion.

fuller.text: The author names the pattern the blessings of scale: in deep learning, bigger often makes hard problems easier. His tentative explanation is that a big network holds countless small sub-networks that average out, favouring simple solutions. Small models settle for memorising, but GPT-3's data has too many sums to memorise, so learning real arithmetic becomes the simpler route.

fuller.text: To show why next-word prediction can demand understanding, the piece tracks error in bits per character, where lower means better guesses. Matching how often letters and spaces appear cuts the error from 8 bits to about 5. Learning real words, spelling and punctuation brings it down to 3 or 4 bits. Humans reach about 0.7 bits, and the author argues the last bits need reasoning, common sense and theory of mind.

fuller.text: The author admits this argument long felt to him like a magic trick. It might have needed more text than exists, or far bigger models, or a different design entirely. He estimates GPT-3's error at about 1.73, and a model 100 to 1,000 times bigger at about 1.24, still short of humans. What new abilities that drop would bring, he says, nobody knows.

fuller.text: The essay contrasts research labs. DeepMind, he argues, holds a weak version: intelligence must be built module by module, copying the brain. OpenAI instead made a startup-style bet that the strong version is true. He criticises expert doubters for a calm voice of authority that makes no checkable predictions and never admits being wrong.

fuller.text: The conclusion is that the scaling hypothesis now looks right, matching Hans Moravec's 1998 forecast of human-rivalling compute in the 2020s. An appendix adds a warning: agency, meaning goal-seeking behaviour, may emerge even without human-made training data. So the author holds that "tool" AIs may become agent AIs, and filtering data is not a fix.

brief.text: The author argues this supports the scaling hypothesis. That is the idea that simple AI may get smarter just by growing much bigger. He says most experts did not predict this and rarely admit they were wrong. If he is right, AI may improve very fast in the 2020s.
